title: Microsoft's (NASDAQ: MSFT) $677 Billion Backlog Makes The Case For A 24.6% Rally Despite Anthropic Pressure - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 16, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A signed commercial backlog of $677 billion gives Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) a visibility advantage that the market appears to be discounting as competitive noise crowds the headlines. Shares have drifted to around $521, sitting roughly 6.8% below the 52-week high of $559.15, even as the underlying business continues to post results well ahead of Wall Street’s expectations. The stock actually traded at $532.60 the day the October 28 earnings report landed, meaning the subsequent slide has erased those post-earnings gains and then some. Sentiment turned after Anthropic unveiled productivity tools that compete directly with Microsoft Office, including a rival to Excel, prompting MarketWatch to label Microsoft the biggest drag on the Dow. Over the past week alone, shares dropped 6.26%, adding to a 3.72% monthly decline, though the stock still holds an 8.41% gain for the year to date. The selloff looks disconnected from what the numbers actually show: fiscal Q1 2027 revenue came in at $92.279 billion, an 18.8% increase that cleared the $90.75 billion analyst estimate by a meaningful margin. Non-GAAP earnings per share of $4.89 also topped the $4.72 consensus, while operating cash flow surged 28.73% to $58 billion, and management expects free cash flow to remain positive for the full fiscal year. Azure’s 48% growth last quarter was the engine, and CFO Amy Hood signaled further acceleration, saying “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” with the division guided to expand 49% to 50% in constant currency during fiscal Q2. Beyond cloud infrastructure, foundry revenue more than tripled in the quarter, and daily Copilot users climbed nearly 50% compared to the prior quarter, reinforcing the monetization runway for Microsoft’s AI investments. Stacked against its two closest cloud rivals, Microsoft’s financial profile stands out: its 46.78% operating margin dwarfs Alphabet’s (NASDAQ: GOOGL) 32.03% and towers over Amazon’s (NASDAQ: AMZN) 11.16%, while its P/E of 29 sits well below Amazon’s multiple of 37. Google Cloud did grow 103% last quarter, but Alphabet generated negative free cash flow of $9.065 billion in the same period, a constraint that limits its capacity to compete on investment; AWS grew 39% but Amazon’s thin margins compress its valuation appeal. Against that backdrop, 24/7 Wall St. has set a 12-month price target of $648.94 on Microsoft, implying 24.6% upside from current levels, backed by a Buy rating and 90% confidence. The analyst community broadly agrees: 40 analysts rate the stock Buy and 12 rate it Strong Buy, with not one carrying a Sell recommendation on the name. The bull case extends to $748.53, a potential 43.72% return, while even the bear case of $548.36 implies a positive outcome from today’s price. Longer-dated targets from 24/7 Wall St. place the stock at $745.05 in 2028, $853.82 in 2029, and $926.15 by 2030, projections that rest on continued execution of the current AI-driven strategy. The key risks center on a planned calendar-year capital expenditure program of roughly $170 billion, operating margins expected to come in slightly below last year’s levels, and a Windows OEM revenue line guided to fall in the mid-30s percentage range. If Azure delivers on its acceleration guidance and Copilot monetization holds, the backlog alone makes it difficult to argue against the current price as an entry point. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

We just published our list of the 10 Stocks to Buy Following Jensen Huang's Departure, and Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) rounds it out at number 10. For three years, the AI trade had one face. Now it has an interim CEO. On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA's chief executive and board member, hours after nerves gripped investors awaiting the outcome of the board's crisis meeting. CFO Colette Kress is running the chipmaker on an interim basis while the board searches for a permanent successor. Analysts moved fast: Bernstein downgraded the stock to Market Perform and halved its target to $200, Baird cut it to Neutral, and Morgan Stanley dropped it from its Top Pick list. The bigger question is cyclicality, not succession. At about 11x forward earnings, NVIDIA trades far below the S&P 500's roughly 19–20x, even after 106% revenue growth last quarter, a sign the market doubts those earnings will last. That is why money is spreading across the AI ecosystem: custom accelerators, the networking that ties clusters together, the clouds renting out compute, and the equipment that fills data halls. We built our list from U.S.-listed companies that sell alternatives to NVIDIA's products, from AI chips and networking to cloud services and data center equipment. To qualify, a company needed a market cap above $40 billion and Buy ratings from at least 70% of covering analysts. We then took the 10 largest and ranked them by median analyst upside. Microsoft Corporation qualified because Azure rents AI capacity to customers regardless of which chips power it. With a market cap of $3.89 trillion, Buy ratings from 93% of 59 analysts, and a median price target of $635 against a November 13 close of $523.88, the stock offers 21.21% upside, which placed it 10th on our list. Microsoft is one of NVIDIA's biggest customers, and it is turning into one of its quiet competitors. Azure sells AI capacity by the hour, and the customer renting it rarely cares whose chip sits underneath. That gives Microsoft room to fill its data centers with its own Maia accelerators and AMD's new Helios racks as well as NVIDIA hardware. The demand behind that strategy is visible in the fiscal Q1 report from October 28. Azure grew 48%, revenue of $92.3 billion beat estimates, and commercial remaining performance obligations jumped 73% to $677 billion. That is a backlog of contracted cloud demand Microsoft can route to whichever silicon gives it the best economics. The risk is that the build-out runs ahead of the payoff. Capital spending more than doubled to about $39.4 billion in the quarter, and Microsoft still buys heavily from NVIDIA, so it is not yet a clean break. The stock has also lagged the market over the past year. For investors who want AI exposure without picking a chip winner, Microsoft's discipline on that spending is the story, and two well-known investors have taken notice.  opened its new fiscal year with results that underline how quickly enterprise AI demand is translating into cloud revenue. Revenue and earnings exceeded expectations, Azure growth accelerated, and the companys backlog of contracted commercial revenue expanded sharply. For the first time, Microsoft also disclosed Azures revenue in dollar terms. Capital spending rose substantially as the company races to build data center capacity. As one of the largest companies in the Russell 1000, Microsofts results are widely viewed as a gauge of enterprise AI adoption. Revenue grew at a strong double-digit pace compared with the same quarter last year, and operating income and net income also increased. Management said results exceeded its expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share. Microsoft Cloud revenue grew faster than total revenue, with growth accelerating from the previous quarter. The company also introduced a new reporting structure with two operating segments, Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer, replacing its long-standing three-segment model. The Agents and Infra segment brings together Azure, cloud productivity software, business applications and related services. Azure, Microsofts cloud computing platform, grew at an accelerated pace, beating expectations even though some third-party data center capacity deliveries were delayed. Strong demand for AI workloads, including model training and inference, has driven much of this growth. Management guided to similar or slightly faster Azure growth in the next quarter. Azures performance matters because it shows that Microsofts large investments in AI infrastructure are producing revenue. For readers following Bluechip Stocks, Microsoft offers a rare combination of mature, highly profitable businesses and exposure to one of the fastest-growing technology trends. Microsofts commercial remaining performance obligation, which represents contracted revenue not yet recognized, rose sharply compared with a year earlier. A larger backlog provides visibility into future revenue, since much of it reflects long-term commitments from businesses and AI developers. Commercial bookings declined compared with last year, but that reflected unusually large commitments in the prior-year quarter. Microsoft continues to expand its Copilot AI assistant across products. Usage of its combined Copilot experience grew strongly from the previous quarter, and customers consuming Copilot through usage-based billing increased rapidly. GitHub Copilot adoption also contributed to stronger results. Premium versions of Microsofts productivity software are helping lift average revenue per user. Capital expenditures rose substantially compared with a year earlier as Microsoft invests in chips, servers and data centers. The company added many new data centers across several continents during the quarter and expects capital spending to remain elevated in the coming quarter. Management has said demand for AI capacity continues to exceed available supply. Despite this heavy investment, Microsoft continues to generate positive free cash flow and returned a significant amount to investors through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter. The scale of AI infrastructure spending is a key concern. If demand slows or pricing pressure increases, returns on these investments could fall short of expectations. Cloud gross margins have declined as the mix shifts toward AI infrastructure. The Devices and Consumer segment saw revenue decline, reflecting weakness in Windows devices and gaming. Supply chain delays for data center equipment could also limit growth. Microsofts size gives it advantages that few companies can match. It has long-standing relationships with most large enterprises through its productivity software, operating systems and cloud services. This installed base allows Microsoft to introduce AI features to millions of business users quickly, often through products customers already use every day. Its financial strength also allows it to fund massive infrastructure investments while continuing to pay dividends and repurchase shares. These factors help explain why many market watchers treat Microsoft as a primary barometer of enterprise AI adoption. In addition to partnering with external AI developers, Microsoft is developing its own first-party models. The company recently completed pre-training of its next base model and released a structured decision-making model that quickly gained thousands of customers. Building in-house models gives Microsoft more control over costs, capabilities and product integration, and reduces dependence on any single partner. These models are being integrated into Microsofts products, including Copilot, Azure AI services and business applications. Combining proprietary models with access to third-party models on Azure allows Microsoft to offer customers a wide range of options while capturing value from AI usage across its platform. Microsoft is also improving how quickly new AI systems go live in its data centers, reducing the time between equipment arriving and capacity becoming available to customers. Faster deployment helps the company convert its large capital investments into revenue more quickly. Microsofts latest quarter shows strong momentum in Azure, a rapidly growing backlog and expanding Copilot usage. These trends suggest enterprise AI adoption is moving from experimentation to large-scale deployment. The central question is whether Microsoft can sustain this growth while managing the costs of one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in its history. Its results over the coming quarters will remain an important signal for the broader AI market. title: Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Price Prediction: Azure and Copilot keep the tape constructive, but momentum has cooled - Blockchain News
content:
Microsoft (MSFT) is trading at $523.63, just below its 7-day average and beneath its 20-day and 50-day moving averages, while longer-term trend support remains intact above the 200-day average. Rec... Microsoft (MSFT) closed at $523.63, up 0.98% on the day, with a 24-hour range of $518.34 to $528.92. That leaves the stock roughly pinned around its pivot point, but the broader structure is softer than the headline gain suggests: price is sitting below the 7-day, 20-day, 50-day, 12-day EMA and 26-day EMA, while the 200-day average at $461.34 still marks the major longer-term trend floor. That split matters because Microsoft is not trading on a clean breakout. The stock is trying to stabilize after a rebound, but the technicals still show short-term distribution rather than fresh trend expansion. Volume also does not yet confirm the move, with the reported activity running at 0.29x of the 5-day average. The most relevant fundamental update remains Microsoft’s fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on October 28, 2026. Management said Microsoft Cloud revenue surpassed $63 billion, up 30% year over year, while total revenue was $92.3 billion, up 19%. Gross margin dollars rose 17%, gross margin percentage was 68%, and operating income increased 21%, or 22% in constant currency. The company also highlighted a major Copilot update and said automated tasks had nearly doubled since July. Those are the operating drivers investors are likely to keep focusing on: Azure momentum, cloud mix, and whether Copilot turns product engagement into durable monetization. Sell-side commentary has remained constructive. On November 10, 2026, RBC Capital maintained an Outperform rating and a $640 price target ahead of Microsoft’s Ignite event, pointing to Azure acceleration to 48% growth in constant currency in fiscal Q1 2027, alongside momentum in Copilot and E7 products. Stockanalysis.com also cited 58 analysts with a Strong Buy consensus and an average target of $636.12, with a low of $440 and a high of $870. Those targets frame the street view as still positive, but they do not change the fact that the stock is currently trading below the cluster of shorter-term trend measures. The moving-average stack is the key signal here. Microsoft’s SMA 7 is $524.14, essentially on top of spot, but the SMA 20 at $528.64 and SMA 50 at $527.87 sit above current price. That keeps the short-term bias under pressure. The 200-day average at $461.34 remains far below spot, so the longer-term trend has not broken down. Live (1m): $517.83  Δ -0.0700 (-0.01%) · 05:31:00 AM Momentum is mixed to slightly weak. Daily RSI is 47.98, which is neutral, while MACD is -0.9330 and the histogram is flat at 0.0000, suggesting momentum has stalled rather than accelerated. Stochastic readings at 34.51 for %K and 27.61 for %D also fit a market that is neither oversold enough to force a reflex rally nor strong enough to claim a sustained uptrend. The key levels are straightforward:
- Immediate resistance: $528.92
- Strong resistance: $534.21
- Immediate support: $518.34
- Strong support: $513.05 Bollinger positioning reinforces that range. The middle band is $528.64, the upper band is $549.47, and the lower band is $507.81. Spot at $523.63 sits below the middle band but above the lower band, so the stock is mid-range rather than stretched. Binance perpetual futures data points to a guarded stance rather than aggressive bullish conviction. Funding is positive at 0.0322%, which means longs are paying shorts. That often signals a mild bullish tilt in positioning, but it is not a standalone conviction gauge. Open interest tells a different story. Real-time open interest is 38,449.16 contracts, with daily open interest value at $19.0 million and a 24-hour decline of 6.60%. That looks more like position closing or liquidation than fresh leverage building. The long/short ratios lean short: Binance global accounts show 43.1% long and 56.9% short, while top traders are 43.3% long and 56.7% short. Taker flow is close to balanced, with a 1.0514 buy/sell ratio, so there is no decisive order-flow imbalance forcing a directional read. The burden of proof is now on Microsoft to reclaim the area around $528.64 to $528.92, then clear $534.21. If that happens on better volume, the stock would start repairing the short-term distribution pattern and open a cleaner path back toward the higher analyst targets. If price loses $518.34, the market is likely to retest $513.05. A break there would put the lower Bollinger band at $507.81 in play and would show that the bounce is failing to convert into a durable trend. The longer-term structure would still not be damaged unless the market starts threatening the 200-day average, but the near-term tone would weaken further. For now, MSFT stock looks like a fundamentally strong name with supportive analyst targets and a solid cloud/Copilot narrative, but the tape is still asking for confirmation.
